people.name: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice
people.summary: Born 21 October 1872 and baptised at Ward End, Aston, on 19 June 1873, son of William and Fanny Mary Fitzmaurice. An engineer all his working life. He married Edith Madeline Spencer at St Matthew's, Brixton, on 2 August 1897. He lived in Cape Town from 1916 to about 1923. He died on 7 June 1928, probably aged 55, and was buried at Chingford Mount. He was not a son of the Earls of Orkney.
people.story: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice was born on 21 October 1872 and baptised on 19 June 1873 at St Margaret's, Ward End, Aston. The register names his parents as William and Fanny Mary Fitzmaurice, of Ward End, and his father as a surveyor and contractor.[^parish-wardend-1873] His own marriage register names that father as Robert William Fitzmaurice, a contractor.[^parish-brixton-1897] The birth index gives his mother's maiden name as Falcke.[^gro-indexes] In 1881 he is the boy written as Ernest Dixon, aged 8, born at Little Bromwich, in the household of Robert William FitzMaurice and Fanny Mary at Aston Manor.[^census-1881-aston] In 1891 he was an apprentice civil engineer, a lodger at 25 Compton Avenue, Brighton, born at Ward End.[^census-1891-brighton] On 2 August 1897, aged 25 and a professional singer, he married Edith Madeline Spencer at St Matthew's, Brixton, by banns.[^parish-brixton-1897] He was probably a civil mechanical engineer in Brixton in 1901.[^census-1901-brixton] In 1911 he was a civil engineer at Whitstable, with Edith and three children.[^census-1911-whitstable] In the middle of the First World War, by then a civil engineer of about 43, he sailed from London for South Africa on the Balmoral Castle on 29 March 1916, meaning to settle there.[^passenger-1916-balmoral] Five months later Edith probably followed on the Llanstephan Castle with Bob, Reg and Eileen.[^passenger-1916-llanstephan] He came back to England in October 1923, giving Whitstable as his address, and sailed for Cape Town again that December.[^passenger-1923-armadale] [^passenger-1923-arundel] Edith came home in November 1925.[^passenger-1925-edith] He died on 7 June 1928, probably aged 55, and was buried at Chingford Mount Cemetery.[^findagrave-214209661] [^burial-chingford-1928] When Eileen married in 1936, the paper remembered him as formerly of Cape Town.[^news-1936-simmons] Edward was an engineer all his working life: an apprentice civil engineer in 1891, a civil engineer in 1901 and 1911, and an engineer on every passenger list from 1916 to 1923. The white collar in the beach photo is not a sign that he was a clergyman.[^beach-snapshots] He was not a son of the Hon. Henry Warrender FitzMaurice. The London Gazette of 23 April 1890 names the 7th Earl of Orkney's surviving brother and sister, and Edward is not among them.[^gazette-1890]

people.name: Edith Madeline FitzMaurice
people.summary: Reg's mother, not his sister. Edith Madeline Spencer married Edward Dixon FitzMaurice on 2 August 1897. She was probably born about 1866 to 1869 in Islington. She probably died in the Bridge district of Kent in early 1929, aged 61. She was probably in South Africa from about 1916 to 1925.
people.story: The medallion portrait inscribed Edith Madeleine Fitzmaurice, about 1899, is Edith Madeline Spencer, Edward Dixon's wife and Reg's mother. Earlier pages that called her Reg's sister were wrong.[^edith-medallion] [^parish-brixton-1897] She was probably born about 1866 to 1869 in Islington. In 1891 she was 22, a governess, born in Islington, living with her widowed mother Caroline at 15 Mornington Place, St Pancras. The house number may read 15b.[^census-1891-spencer] Her death in 1929, aged 61, fits that birth. At the wedding she was recorded as 24, and in 1911 as 38 and born at St Anne, Soho. Those later ages are the odd ones out. Her birth registration has not been found. A birth of Edith Maria Spencer at Islington in 1866 belongs to a different family and is not hers.[^census-1891-spencer] [^gro-edith-death] [^census-1911-whitstable] On 2 August 1897 she married Edward at St Matthew's, Brixton. Her father, Charles Spencer, a builder and contractor, was already dead. Caroline Spencer was a witness.[^parish-brixton-1897] In 1911, at Whitstable, she and Edward had had four children, of whom three were living. The child who had died was Edith Marjorie.[^census-1911-whitstable] She probably died in the March quarter of 1929 in the Bridge district of Kent, aged 61.[^gro-edith-death] She probably went out to Cape Town in August 1916 with Bob, Reg and Eileen. At the end of 1923 she came to London with Reg and Eileen on the Bendigo, landing on 28 December 1923, and gave 140A Clapham Road, London S.W. (the number is hard to read).[^passenger-1923-bendigo] She came back to England from South Africa in November 1925, aged 53 by her own account, giving Birkenhead as her destination.[^passenger-1916-llanstephan] [^passenger-1925-edith]

people.name: Baron Reginald FitzMaurice
people.summary: Pat's father. Baron is his forename, not a title. Probably born on 26 May 1904 in the Wandsworth district, son of Edward Dixon and Edith Madeline. He probably married Lilian Maud Mary Bennett in late 1927. He died on 31 March 1977.
people.story: Reg was Baron Reginald FitzMaurice. Baron is a forename, not a title. He was probably born on 26 May 1904 in the Wandsworth district. The birth index names his mother as Spenser, a spelling of Spencer, volume 1d, page 670.[^gro-indexes] [^probate-reg-1977] In 1911 he is Baron Reginald, aged 6, at school, in Edward Dixon and Edith Madeline's household at Whitstable.[^census-1911-whitstable] He probably married Lilian Maud Mary Bennett in the December quarter of 1927, in the Hammersmith district, volume 1a, page 661.[^gro-marriage-1927] Electoral registers place him in Wandsworth in 1925 and 1926, Hammersmith from 1931 to 1933, the Spelthorne district from 1934 to 1937, and Hayes from 1938 until about 1972.[^electoral-fitzmaurice] On 11 February 1950 he gave his daughter Patricia away at St Mary's, Wanstead. The album calls him Mr R. Fitzmaurice of Hayes.[^album-1950] He died on 31 March 1977. The death was registered at Hillingdon, and the probate calendar places him at Hayes. The estate was 24,427 pounds.[^probate-reg-1977] A cause of death remembered in the family is not on the certificate we have, so it is not stated here. A studio portrait of a young man in a bow tie has no name on it, and it is not identified as Reg. He was probably the boy of 12 on the same voyage to Cape Town in August 1916.[^passenger-1916-llanstephan] He came back to London with his mother and Eileen on the Bendigo, landing on 28 December 1923, listed as Baron Fitzmaurice, a student, aged 19.[^passenger-1923-bendigo]

people.summary: Pat's mother. Lilian Maud Mary Bennett, born about March 1900 at Bodmin, the youngest daughter of Charles Bennett and Annie, nee Grigg, who survived childhood. She probably died in the Uxbridge district in late 1947, aged 47.
people.story: The wedding album's late Mrs R. Fitzmaurice was probably Lilian Maud Mary Bennett. She was born about March 1900 at Bodmin, Cornwall. The birth index, June quarter 1900, volume 5c, page 64, names her mother as Grigg, and the 1921 census gives the same three forenames, aged 21 years and 3 months, born at Bodmin.[^gro-lilian-death] [^census-1921-lilian] [^census-bennett] Her parents were Charles Bennett, a tailor of Egloshayle and Bodmin, and Annie, probably Matilda Ann Nicholls Grigg. Lilian was the youngest of the children who survived. In June 1921 she was a clerk at the Claims Record Office, boarding at Hampton Hill.[^census-1921-lilian] She probably married Baron Reginald FitzMaurice in the December quarter of 1927, in the Hammersmith district.[^gro-marriage-1927] She probably died in the December quarter of 1947, in the Uxbridge district, which covered Hayes, aged 47.[^gro-lilian-death] The album of February 1950 therefore calls her the late Mrs R. Fitzmaurice.[^album-1950] No will and no grave have been found. A family memory that she died while Pat was a young child does not fit an age of about 18.

people.name: Edward Robert FitzMaurice
people.summary: Reg's brother, called Bob. Edward Robert FitzMaurice, born in the Lambeth district in 1901. He married in Cape Town in 1925 and died at Port Elizabeth on 7 May 1981.
people.story: The beach photograph is labelled Reg, Bob and their father Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice. Bob is Edward Robert Fitzmaurice, mother's maiden name Spencer, registered in the Lambeth district in the June quarter of 1901, volume 1d, page 503. In 1911 he was 9, at school, at Whitstable. He was probably the boy of 15 who sailed to Cape Town with his mother in August 1916. On 30 October 1925, aged 24, a tramway engineer, he married Eileen Alice Yallop at St George's Cathedral, Cape Town. He was living at Auleta, Three Anchor Bay, and she at 7 Bertram Road, Sea Point. In 1926 their home was 17 Berkley Street, Gardens, when their son Edward Scott was baptised in the parish of Woodstock. Edward Scott died on 9 August 1935, aged 9, at Somerset Hospital. The home was then given as 1st Avenue, Bellville. Edward Robert died on 7 May 1981 at Port Elizabeth.

people.name: Henry George Andrews
people.summary: Ron's father. Henry George Andrews, born at St Albans in April 1889, only child of Herbert Andrews and Lucy Stacey. He married Rosina Maud Cousins on 18 April 1915. He, Rosina and their son Sidney were killed at their home in Plaistow on 19 April 1941.
people.story: Henry George Andrews was born at St Albans, Hertfordshire, in April 1889, and baptised at St Albans Abbey on 9 June 1889, son of Herbert and Lucy.[^parish-st-albans-1889] The birth index names his mother as Stacey.[^gro-indexes] He was their only child.[^census-andrews-stacey] In 1901 the family was at Hemel Hempstead. In 1911 he was a sawyer's labourer, living with his parents at Canning Town. On 18 April 1915, aged 25, he married Rosina Maud Cousins at St Andrew's, Plaistow. His father is Herbert Andrews. Hers is William Cousins.[^parish-plaistow-1915] In 1921 he was a dock labourer for the Port of London Authority at the Royal Albert Docks, living at Plaistow in his father-in-law's house. In 1939 he was an explosive worker at the Royal filling factory, Woolwich.[^census-cousins] [^register-1939] He was killed on 19 April 1941, aged 52, at the family home in Plaistow, in the West Ham county borough, together with Rosina and their son Sidney.[^cwgc-plaistow-1941] The wedding album's East Ham is the neighbouring borough. The Commonwealth War Graves record gives Plaistow.

people.story: Rosina Maud Cousins was born on 14 November 1881 at Bermondsey, and registered in the St Olave district, volume 1d, page 292. Her mother's maiden name was Gall.[^gro-cousins-gall] She was one of eight children of William Cousins, a dock labourer born at Hackney, and Annie, nee Gall, born at Thetford.[^census-cousins] On 18 April 1915 she married Henry George Andrews at St Andrew's, Plaistow.[^parish-plaistow-1915] Their children were Herbert William, Ronald and Sidney George. The home in Plaistow had been her father's. She, Henry and Sidney were killed there on 19 April 1941. Rosina was 59.[^cwgc-plaistow-1941]

people.summary: Son of Henry George Andrews and Rosina Maud Cousins. Probably born in the summer of 1921 in the West Ham district. He married Patricia Mary FitzMaurice on 11 February 1950. people.story: Ronald Andrews was probably born in the summer of 1921 in the West Ham district, son of Henry George Andrews and Rosina Maud Cousins, and brother of Herbert William and Sidney George.[^family-testimony] He married Patricia Mary FitzMaurice at St Mary's, Wanstead, on 11 February 1950.[^album-1950] He is the father of Amanda and Venetia. His wartime photograph album has its own page. The press card names him Leading Aircraftman R. Andrews, art editor of the Tura Times, the newspaper of No. 111 Maintenance Unit, in 1945.[^ron-album] He died in 2010 (family).[^family-testimony] Pat died in 2020 (family). Pat and Ron are buried together in the churchyard of St John the Baptist Parish Church, Waterloo Road, Crowthorne, Berkshire (family).[^st-john-crowthorne-churchyard] No home address is published.

people.name: Cecil FitzMaurice, 8th Earl of Orkney
people.summary: A distant cousin of the 7th Earl, he inherited the earldom in 1951 while serving as an Army driver in Korea. He married Rose Silley at Brixham in 1953.
people.story: Cecil O'Bryen FitzMaurice was the younger son of Douglas Frederick Harold FitzMaurice and Dorothy Dickie. He joined the Royal Army Service Corps in 1939 and served in North Africa, Italy, France and Germany, and then in Korea.[^wiki-cecil][^peerage-cecil] He became the 8th Earl of Orkney on 21 August 1951 while serving as a driver in Korea. Newspapers called him "the Earl from Korea".[^press-1951][^korea-clipping] The Evening News reported that his Army friends knew him as "Ginger", that the 7th Earl had left him the residue of an estate of £42,893, and that on the voyage home he was given four days' confinement to barracks and set to scrub the mess decks for coming back late to the ship at Colombo.[^korea-clipping] The paper called the 7th Earl his great-uncle; he was in fact a much more distant cousin.[^korea-clipping][^peerage-cecil] On 27 November 1953 he married Rose Katherine Durk Silley at St Mary's, Brixham. The Evening News said she helped her mother run a 60-bedroom hotel in the town, and that the Earl had once worked in a garage.[^marries-clipping][^peerage-cecil] Rose died in 1995. Cecil died in February 1998 with no children, and the earldom passed to a distant cousin, Peter St John.[^wiki-cecil][^wiki-earl-of-orkney] Earlier pages give the year of his marriage as 1952. The peerage records give 1953.[^site-earlier][^peerage-cecil] ## Link to this family Earlier versions of this site traced Sebastian's line to this person through Edward Dixon FitzMaurice. That link is not proven, and the 1890 London Gazette record speaks against it (see Edward Dixon FitzMaurice). This person is shown in a separate frame for that reason.[^gazette-1890][^site-earlier]

people.summary: Clerk in the Board of Ordnance at the Tower of London. He married Eliza Taylor at St Martin's, Birmingham, on 3 February 1827. Father of William, John Richard and Robert William. By 1861 he was described as a gentleman. His birth, parents and death have not been found.
people.story: John FitzMaurice married Eliza Taylor by licence at St Martin's, Birmingham, on 3 February 1827. The register describes him as of His Majesty's Tower of London, a bachelor, and Eliza as of that parish, a spinster. John Taylor witnessed the marriage.[^parish-birmingham-1827] He was a clerk with the Board of Ordnance: a clerk at their son William's baptism in 1827, a clerk in the Ordnance Office in 1829, and a clerk in the Tower in 1832.[^parish-whitechapel-1827] [^parish-stepney-1829] [^parish-stepney-1832] The family lived in Whitechapel and then in Mile End Old Town. By 1861, when Robert William married, the register calls John a gentleman.[^parish-battersea-1861] His own birth, his parents and his death have not been found. A published family history places him in a Carlow branch of the FitzMaurices of Kerry. The London entries in that account now agree with these registers. No record found so far states where he was born or who his parents were, so that origin stays likely but not proved.[^fitzmaurice-family-carlow]

people.name: Eliza FitzMaurice
people.summary: Eliza Taylor of St Martin's parish, Birmingham. She married John FitzMaurice there on 3 February 1827. Mother of William, John Richard and Robert William.
people.story: Eliza Taylor, of the parish of St Martin's, Birmingham, married John FitzMaurice there by licence on 3 February 1827. John Taylor witnessed.[^parish-birmingham-1827] She is named with John at the baptisms of their three sons: William at St Mary's, Whitechapel, on 25 December 1827, John Richard at St Dunstan's, Stepney, on 4 November 1829, and Robert William at the same church on 30 September 1832.[^parish-whitechapel-1827] [^parish-stepney-1829] [^parish-stepney-1832] She was of Birmingham, which is probably why their son Robert William later settled there. Her birth and death have not been found.

people.name: William G. Falcke
people.summary: Potter at Battersea, born abroad about 1793. Father of Fanny Mary. Buried at St Mary's, Battersea, on 27 August 1849, aged 56.
people.story: William Gottlob Falcke was born abroad about 1793. The 1841 census records him as a potter at Battersea, born in foreign parts.[^census-1841-falcke] He married Eliza Macfarlin at St Mary's, Battersea, on 15 October 1817. On their children's baptisms she is Elizabeth. They had ten children baptised at Chelsea and Battersea between 1818 and 1837. Fanny Mary, baptised in 1837, was the youngest.[^parish-falcke-1817] [^parish-battersea-1837] He was buried at St Mary's, Battersea, on 27 August 1849, aged 56.[^burial-falcke-1849] By 1861, when Fanny married, he was described as a manufacturer.[^parish-battersea-1861]

people.name: Robert W. FitzMaurice
people.summary: Baptised 30 September 1832 at St Dunstan's, Stepney, son of John and Eliza. Surveyor, later a granite merchant and contractor. Married Fanny Mary Falcke in 1861. Died 10 May 1895 at Edgbaston.
people.story: Robert William FitzMaurice was baptised on 30 September 1832 at St Dunstan's, Stepney, son of John, a clerk in the Tower, and Eliza. The date usually given as his birth is this baptism. He was the youngest of three sons. William was born in 1827 and John Richard was baptised in 1829.[^parish-stepney-1832] [^parish-whitechapel-1827] [^parish-stepney-1829] On 14 September 1861, a surveyor, he married Fanny Mary Falcke at St Mary's, Battersea. His father John is called a gentleman on that register.[^parish-battersea-1861] In 1871 he was a surveyor and contractor at Little Bromwich, Aston, born in Stepney.[^census-1871-aston] In 1881 he was a granite merchant and contractor at Aston Manor.[^census-1881-aston] He died at Edgbaston on 10 May 1895, aged 64. His estate was 12,921 pounds 4 shillings and 9 pence. The executors were his widow Fanny Mary and their sons John Rupert, a quarry owner, and Walter, a contractor.[^probate-robert-1895] When his son Edward married in 1897, the register names Robert William Fitzmaurice, contractor, as the father, and says he was already dead.[^parish-brixton-1897]

people.story: Fanny Mary was born on 3 December 1836 and baptised at St Mary's, Battersea, on 29 January 1837, as Mary Fanny, daughter of William Gottlob Falcke, a potter, and Elizabeth.[^parish-battersea-1837] She is in the family at Battersea in 1841 and, aged 14, with her mother in 1851.[^census-1841-falcke] [^census-1851-falcke] On 14 September 1861 she married Robert William FitzMaurice at the same church. The register calls her father a manufacturer.[^parish-battersea-1861] A line in the 1871 census that gives her birthplace as France is a mistake. The baptism, the 1851 census and the 1881 census all give Battersea.[^census-1871-aston] [^census-1881-aston] She died at Erdington on 25 October 1917, aged 80.[^probate-fanny-1917] She was probably the mother of Edward Dixon: his birth index names the mother's maiden name as Falcke, and she was Robert William's wife.[^gro-indexes]

people.name: Caroline Spencer

people.story: Caroline was Edith Madeline's mother. In 1891, a widow, she was a lodging house keeper at 15 Mornington Place, St Pancras (the house number may read 15b), born in Islington, aged 44, with her daughter Edith, a governess of 22.[^census-1891-spencer] She witnessed Edith's marriage in 1897.[^parish-brixton-1897] In 1901 she was probably living with Edith and Edward in Brixton, recorded as about 52.[^census-1901-brixton] The ages put her birth about 1843 to 1849, in Islington. An 1881 entry sometimes suggested for her has not been shown to be the same woman, and it is not used here. Her maiden name and her death have not been found.

people.story: Edith Marjorie Fitzmaurice, mother's maiden name Spencer, was registered in the Greenwich district in the December quarter of 1899, volume 1d, page 1075.[^gro-indexes] She died in the September quarter of 1900 in the Lewisham district, volume 1d, page 707, aged under a year.[^gro-indexes] The 1911 census says four children had been born to Edward and Edith and one had died. She is that child.[^census-1911-whitstable] She did not grow up, so she is not the woman in the medallion portrait.

people.summary: Reg's younger sister, called Auntie Babs (confirmed by the family). Born late 1907 in the Blean district of Kent, daughter of Edward Dixon and Edith Madeline. She probably sailed to Cape Town in 1916, married Leslie Hugh Simmons at Staines in the summer of 1936, and probably died at Canterbury in early 1996.
people.story: The youngest of Edward Dixon and Edith's children, Eileen was 3 at Whitstable in 1911.[^census-1911-whitstable] She was probably the girl of 8 who sailed to Cape Town with her mother and brothers in August 1916.[^passenger-1916-llanstephan] She came back to London from South Africa with her mother and Reg on the Bendigo, landing on 28 December 1923, aged 16.[^passenger-1923-bendigo] A snapshot of a girl on a verandah is labelled on the back Auntie Babs, South Africa, and the letters Eil are scratched into the front. The family confirms she was that girl.[^photo-labels] [^beach-snapshots] She married Leslie Hugh Simmons, secretary of the Corinth Hockey Club, at Staines in the summer of 1936. The local paper called her the daughter of the late Mr Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice, formerly of Cape Town.[^news-1936-simmons] In 1939 the couple lived at Hayes, close to her brother Reg. Leslie was a rate fixer and motion study engineer.[^register-1939] As Auntie Babs she was at Pat's wedding in 1950, with Uncle Leslie beside her.[^album-1950] In 1984 she married Ralph Hallawell in Kent, and she probably died at Canterbury in early 1996, aged 88.[^gro-indexes]

people.summary: Lilian's father. A tailor, later a general labourer, then a tailor and outfitter, born at Egloshayle in Cornwall about 1850. He and Annie were living apart in 1911. He probably died at Bodmin on 5 December 1925, aged 77.
people.story: Charles Bennett was born at Egloshayle, Cornwall, about 1849 to 1851. In 1891 he was a tailor in Bodmin. In 1901 he was a general labourer at 1 Honey Street, Bodmin. In 1911 he was 62, a tailor and outfitter, born at Slades, Egloshayle, and living in Bodmin with his son Frank.[^census-bennett] He and Annie had probably married in 1882, in the Stoke Damerel district.[^gro-bennett-grigg] In 1911 they were living apart in the same town. Annie, who kept a draper's shop, described herself as a widow, but Charles was alive. Both of their census forms say 11 children had been born, 8 were living and 3 had died.[^census-bennett] He probably died at Bodmin on 5 December 1925, aged 77. Administration of his estate, 296 pounds 1 shilling and 4 pence, was granted to May Bennett, a spinster. That grant does not, by itself, show which daughter she was.[^probate-charles-bennett-1926]

She later worked at Ealing, and in 1939 she was a dining hall maid at Colchester.[^census-1921-may] [^register-1939] From 1948 to 1967 the electoral registers place her at Chiswick and Gunnersbury, and then at Feltham.[^electoral-may] She died on 27 September 1971. The estate was 1,541 pounds.[^probate-may-1971] This is the Auntie May Amanda remembered: an elderly aunt who had never married, who came to stay, and who lived at Chiswick. She was probably also the Auntie May named at Pat and Ron's wedding, though that last step is not proved. Lilian's sister Minnie is a different person.

people.about: Bob's wife, born about 1902 in South Africa
people.summary: Bob's wife. Born about 1902 in South Africa. She married him at St George's Cathedral, Cape Town, on 30 October 1925. She was alive in May 1981. No later death record has been found, and she is treated as deceased because of her age.
people.story: Eileen Alice Yallop was 23, born in South Africa, and living at 7 Bertram Road, Sea Point, when she married Edward Robert Fitzmaurice on 30 October 1925 at St George's Cathedral, Cape Town. In 1926 they lived at 17 Berkley Street, Gardens. Their son Edward Scott was born on 29 April 1926 and died in 1935. She is named as Edward Robert's spouse on his 1981 death index, so she was alive in May 1981. No record of her own death has been found. She was born about 1902, so the ledger treats her as deceased.

birth.note: Aged 23 at the marriage on 30 October 1925, born in South Africa. No death record has been found. She was alive in May 1981, and the ledger treats her as deceased because she was born about 1902.

sections.heading: Grandma Pat and Grandpa Ron, and the families they came from
sections.text: This site follows both families back from the photographs they kept to the records behind them: where they lived, what they did, and how everyone is connected.

sections.heading: How this started
sections.text: It started with a large collection of family photographs. I took pictures of a handful that caught my eye: a studio portrait from Knightsbridge, a small medallion with a name written on the back, a beach snapshot labelled in pencil, two newspaper cuttings that Pat had kept, and the album from Pat and Ron’s wedding. Each one gave up a little more. A studio’s address, a name on the back of a card or a date in a cutting led to the records: the census, the indexes of births, marriages and deaths, parish registers, probate, passenger lists and army service files. One record led to the next, and every finding was checked against the record before it went in.

sections.heading: How this started
sections.text: Over time it became a family tree of nearly a hundred people across eight generations, a map of the places they lived and worked, and a page for each branch of the family. Every claim links to the record behind it, so you can look at the original for yourself. Not every family story held up. Pat kept the cuttings about Cecil FitzMaurice, who became the 8th Earl of Orkney while he was serving in Korea, and the family believed we were connected. The records do not show a descent from the Earls of Orkney. Cecil may still be a relative somewhere on Pat’s side, so he stays on the tree beside her, joined only by a dashed line marked suspected relative.

sections.heading: The two families
sections.text: On the family tree, Ron’s family is on the left and Pat’s is on the right. The two sides meet at the wedding.

sections.heading: Grandpa Ron’s family
sections.text: Andrews, Stacey, Walter and Cousins. The Andrews family were farm workers and bakers from Totternhoe in Bedfordshire, who moved to Aldenham in Hertfordshire in the 1870s. Ron’s father, Henry George Andrews, was born at St Albans in 1889. He married Rosina Maud Cousins, from Bermondsey, in 1915, and served in France in the First World War. Their home was in Plaistow, in West Ham, and Ron was born in the West Ham district in 1921, between his brothers Herbert and Sidney. On 19 April 1941 Henry George, Rosina and Sidney were killed at their home in the Blitz. Ron served with the RAF in Egypt, working on aircraft engines in the caves at Tura.

sections.heading: Grandma Pat’s family
sections.text: FitzMaurice, Falcke, Spencer and Bennett. Pat’s FitzMaurice line goes back to John FitzMaurice, a clerk in the Board of Ordnance at the Tower of London, who married Eliza Taylor at Birmingham in 1827. His son Robert William married Fanny Mary Falcke, from a Battersea family. Their son Edward Dixon FitzMaurice, born at Aston in 1872, was a civil engineer. He married Edith Madeline Spencer at Brixton in 1897, and in 1916 he went to work for the Cape Electric Tramways in Cape Town, where the family followed him. Their son Reg, Pat’s father, probably married Lilian Maud Mary Bennett, a tailor’s daughter from Bodmin in Cornwall, in late 1927. Pat was born in early 1929, probably in the Hammersmith district. Ron and Pat married at St Mary’s Church, Wanstead, on Saturday 11 February 1950. See the wedding album.

sections.heading: The photographs that started it
sections.text: Some of the original photographs from the collection, and what each one led to. Select a picture to see it larger.

sections.heading: Camden Town, c. 1865
sections.text: The earliest photograph in the collection was taken at J. Perriman's studio near the Mother Red Cap pub in Camden Town. Neither sitter is named. The card does not show where the family came from. Edward Dixon's parents married at Battersea, and their children were born in Birmingham. The reverse reads: 'Camden Town School of Photography, Commission No. 925.'.

sections.heading: Edith Madeleine FitzMaurice, c. 1899
sections.text: A circular medallion portrait inscribed on the reverse 'Edith Madeleine Fitzmaurice c.1899.' She was Reg's mother, Edith Madeline Spencer, not his sister. She was probably born about 1866 to 1869 in Islington, married Edward Dixon FitzMaurice at St Matthew's, Brixton, on 2 August 1897, and probably died in the Bridge district of Kent in early 1929, aged 61. Her age is not the same in every record. Her children.

sections.heading: Edward Dixon in Knightsbridge
sections.text: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice was born on 21 October 1872 and baptised on 19 June 1873 at St Margaret's, Ward End, Aston. The register names both parents, William and Fanny Mary Fitzmaurice. The Stuart studio portrait is probably Edward Dixon, by his likeness to the labelled beach photo. Edward was an engineer all his working life: an apprentice civil engineer in 1891, a civil engineer in 1901 and 1911, and an engineer on every passenger list from 1916 to 1923. The white collar in the beach photo is not a sign that he was a clergyman. On 2 August 1897, a professional singer aged 25, he married Edith Madeline Spencer at St Matthew's, Brixton. He died on 7 June 1928, probably aged 55, and was buried at Chingford Mount Cemetery. His engineering career and the South Africa years are on the Falcke page. His father was Robert William FitzMaurice and his mother was Fanny Mary Falcke.

sections.heading: Probably Edith, Brixton
sections.text: The same young woman, in the same jewelled headband, pearl necklace and flowered costume, appears on the medallion inscribed Edith Madeleine Fitzmaurice c.1899. The Lang Sims studio was on Brixton Road, close to St Matthew's, Brixton, where Edith married Edward Dixon in 1897. The costume looks theatrical. Edward gave his occupation as professional singer at the wedding.

sections.heading: A young man in a bow tie
sections.text: This portrait has no name on it. It is not identified as Reg. Reg himself was Baron Reginald FitzMaurice. Baron is a forename, not a title. He was probably born on 26 May 1904 in the Wandsworth district, probably married Lilian Maud Mary Bennett in late 1927, and died on 31 March 1977. The probate calendar places him at Hayes.

sections.heading: Reg, Bob and their father
sections.text: The reverses of two photographs confirm key family identities. One reads 'Reg, Bob and their Father Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice.' The other reads 'Auntie Babs, South Africa.' The 1911 census bears out what the label says: Reg and Bob were Edward Dixon's sons. The beach snapshot was probably taken about 1908 to 1910 on the Kent coast, when the family lived near Whitstable. Bob would have been about 7 and Reg about 4. Reg made a short trip to Canada early in 1925: see Reg's page. Two unlabelled snapshots, a house with a verandah and a young man in a dark suit, may date from the family's South African years, about 1916 to 1925, but nothing on them says so.

sections.heading: Auntie Babs, the girl in South Africa
sections.text: A snapshot of a girl on a verandah is labelled on the back in pencil: Auntie Babs, South Africa. The letters Eil are scratched into the front. The family confirms she was Eileen Sybil FitzMaurice, Reg's younger sister, born in Kent in late 1907. In March 1916 her father, Edward Dixon, an engineer, sailed for South Africa to make a new life there, and that August a Mrs FitzMaurice of 43 followed with two boys of 15 and 12 and a girl of 8, the ages of Edith, Bob, Reg and Eileen. When Eileen married Leslie Hugh Simmons at Staines in the summer of 1936, the local paper called her the daughter of the late Mr Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice, formerly of Cape Town. Fourteen years later Auntie Babs and Uncle Leslie stood side by side on the steps at Pat and Ron's wedding. Babs lived with Reg and Lilian in the early 1930s: see Eileen's entry.

sections.heading: The Korean War Earl
sections.text: Among Pat's papers were two Evening News cuttings about Cecil FitzMaurice. The first says that he became the 8th Earl of Orkney in August 1951 while he was serving as an Army driver in Korea, that he was set to scrub the mess decks on the voyage home after returning late to the ship at Colombo, and that he was left the residue of a £42,893 estate. The second reports his marriage to Rose Silley at Brixham in November 1953. Pat kept both, and the family believed there was a connection.

sections.heading: The Korean War Earl
sections.text: The records do not show that we descend from the Earls of Orkney: the London Gazette of 23 April 1890 rules that out. Cecil may still be a relative somewhere on Pat's side, so he stays on the family tree beside her as a suspected relative, with no proven link. Our FitzMaurice line goes back to John FitzMaurice, a clerk in the Board of Ordnance at the Tower of London, who married Eliza Taylor at Birmingham in 1827. A published family history places John in a Carlow branch of the FitzMaurices of Kerry. If that is right, the Earls were distant cousins. That link is likely but not yet proved.

sections.heading: The Andrews Family, c. 1930s
sections.text: The photograph has no label, so the names come from family memory, and the caption names the father twice. The records name the parents as Henry George Andrews and Rosina Maud Cousins, and the younger son as Sidney George. All three were killed at their home in Plaistow on 19 April 1941. The album's East Ham is the next borough. Herbert William, the elder brother, was born in 1916. The Andrews line and the Cousins line. Update, November 2026: The photograph has no label, so these names come from family memory. The caption names the father twice, once in each row; only one of those can be right.

sections.heading: The Photo Collection Spread
sections.text: The wider collection of photographs and cabinet cards laid out together. Additional postcards, unidentified portraits, and snapshots from across the family's history, many still waiting to be identified. Probable claims are worded with probably, about or likely. Anyone who may still be living is named with a first name and a relationship only. Sources, and how a claim is worded.

sections.heading: The family branches
sections.text: These pages follow the lines that the records support: FitzMaurice and Falcke, Reg's brother and sisters, the Bennetts of Bodmin, the Andrews, Stacey and Walter families, and the Cousins family, including Auntie May. Words such as probably, about and likely mark a claim that the records point to, but that a certificate would still make firmer. How the evidence is graded.

sections.heading: The family branches
sections.text: Patricia Andrews, nee FitzMaurice, and Ronald Andrews have both died. Ronald died in 2010 (family). Pat died in 2020 (family). Pat and Ron are buried together in the churchyard of St John the Baptist Parish Church, Waterloo Road, Crowthorne, Berkshire (family). Patricia was probably born in the Hammersmith district in early 1929, and the family remembers Windsor, which is not the registered birthplace. Their years are on the tree. Everyone else who may still be living is named with their relationship only. House numbers are left off. The 1890 London Gazette rules out a descent from that family. A Carlow origin for John FitzMaurice, which would make the earls distant cousins rather than ancestors, is likely but not proved.

sections.heading: Edward Dixon's parents
sections.text: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice was born on 21 October 1872 and baptised at Ward End, Aston, on 19 June 1873. The baptism names his parents as Robert William and Fanny Mary Fitzmaurice, of Ward End. Fanny Mary's maiden name, on the birth index and on her marriage, is Falcke.

sections.heading: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice
sections.text: He was born on 21 October 1872 and baptised on 19 June 1873 at St Margaret's, Ward End, in the parish of Aston. The register names his parents as Robert William and Fanny Mary Fitzmaurice, of Ward End, and his father as a surveyor and contractor. The birth index is the December quarter of 1872 at Aston, volume 6d, page 396, mother Falcke. In the 1881 census Edward appears at Sutton Road, Aston, aged 8, as "Ernest Dixon", the son of Robert William and Fanny Mary. The enumerator wrote Ernest, but the parents, the rare middle name and his age all point to Edward, and no Ernest FitzMaurice birth was registered in those years. In 1891 he was an apprentice civil engineer, a lodger at 25 Compton Avenue, Brighton.

sections.heading: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice
sections.text: On 2 August 1897, aged 25 and a professional singer, he married Edith Madeline Spencer at St Matthew's, Brixton. He was probably a civil mechanical engineer in Brixton in 1901, and in 1911 he was a civil engineer at Whitstable, at Clifton Ville, Westgate Terrace, with Edith and the children Edward Robert, Baron Reginald and Eileen.

sections.heading: Edward Dixon FitzMaurice
sections.text: Edward was an engineer all his working life: an apprentice civil engineer in 1891, a civil engineer in 1901 and 1911, and an engineer on every passenger list from 1916 to 1923. In August 1914 the trade paper Tramway and Railway World reported "Mr. Fitzmaurice, the permanent way engineer of the British Electrical Federation" taking part in a discussion on rail joints. The white collar in the beach photo is not a sign that he was a clergyman. Edward died on 7 June 1928 and was buried six days later, on 13 June, at Chingford Mount Cemetery, section F12. The cemetery register gives his age as 56; by his birth date he was 55. He was not a son of the Earls of Orkney: the London Gazette of 23 April 1890 names the 7th Earl's surviving brother and sister, and Edward is not among them. His own children are on the brother and sisters page.

sections.heading: South Africa, 1916 to about 1925
sections.text: In the middle of the First World War Edward Dixon FitzMaurice, by then a civil engineer of about 43, sailed from London for South Africa on the Balmoral Castle on 29 March 1916, meaning to settle there. In April 1916 Tramway and Railway World announced that Mr. E. D. Fitzmaurice was leaving the British Electrical Federation to join the Cape Electric Tramways in Cape Town. Five months later his wife Edith followed on the Llanstephan Castle with their three children, Bob, Reg and Eileen. That family voyage is probable, because the list gives ages and no first names. Edward's own voyages are on the lists under his name.

sections.heading: South Africa, 1916 to about 1925
sections.text: When he landed at Southampton on 15 October 1923 he gave 14 Waterloo Road, Whitstable as his address, and he sailed back to the Cape from the same address on 21 December. The incoming passenger lists from 1924 to June 1928 show no later voyage home for him, so how and when he finally came back to England before his death is not known. Edith came home in November 1925. When Eileen married in 1936, the paper remembered him as formerly of Cape Town.

sections.heading: John FitzMaurice and Eliza Taylor
sections.text: John FitzMaurice married Eliza Taylor by licence at St Martin's, Birmingham, on 3 February 1827, entry 53. He was of His Majesty's Tower of London, a bachelor. She was of that parish, a spinster. John Taylor and Hannah Taylor witnessed. He was a clerk with the Board of Ordnance: a clerk in 1827, a clerk in the Ordnance Office in 1829, and a clerk in the Tower in 1832. The family lived in Whitechapel, including Mansell Street when William was baptised, and then in Mile End Old Town. By 1861 he was described as a gentleman. His birth, his parents and his death have not been found. A possible baptism for Eliza is at St Philip's, Birmingham, on 2 January 1806: Eliza, daughter of John and Ann Taylor. It is only a candidate. Other Eliza and Elizabeth Taylors with a father named John were baptised in Birmingham between 1800 and 1809, and the entry still has to be read on the register image.

sections.heading: John FitzMaurice and Eliza Taylor
sections.text: Eliza was of Birmingham. That is probably why their son Robert William later settled there. Her own birth and death have not been found.

sections.heading: Their three sons
sections.text: William, the eldest, was born on 23 December 1827 and baptised the next day, Christmas Day, at St Mary's, Whitechapel. The family were then at Mansell Street, and John was a clerk. John Richard was baptised on 4 November 1829 at St Dunstan's, Stepney, entry 1006. The family were of Mile End Old Town, and John was a clerk in the Ordnance Office. The date is the baptism, not a recorded birth. Robert William, the youngest, was baptised on 30 September 1832 at the same church, entry 1537. John was then a clerk in the Tower. The date is the baptism. A family history that says he was born that day is copying the baptism.

sections.heading: A Carlow origin, likely but not proved
sections.text: A published family history places John in a Carlow branch of the FitzMaurices of Kerry. It says he was born on 6 July 1803, son of John FitzMaurice of Kelvin Grove, Killeshin, County Carlow, and Henrietta Frances Cary. The London part of that account now agrees with the registers: Eliza Taylor, the three sons, and William's date of birth. It also names a brother, Robert Thomas, as a clerk in the Ordnance Office. On 13 October 1859, at St John the Evangelist, Clapham, Robert Thomas Fitz Maurice, gentleman, is named as the father of Emma Frances when she married Samuel Dixon, a merchant. Emma Frances was a first cousin of Robert William, and she is possibly the source of the name Dixon in Edward Dixon. That is a real man in the same office. No record found so far says where John was born, or who his parents were. The Carlow origin is likely, and it is not yet proved. It is not drawn on the tree.

sections.heading: Robert William FitzMaurice
sections.text: Baptised 30 September 1832, St Dunstan's, Stepney, entry 1537. Died 10 May 1895, 16 York Road, Edgbaston. On 2 October 1858, three years before their own wedding, Robert William and Fanny Mary both signed as witnesses when her sister Jane married John Peacock Turner at St Mary's, Battersea. On census night in April 1861 Robert William, 29 and unmarried, was a visitor in a lodging house in St Marylebone, described as an engineer and contractor. The birthplace written on his line is Norfolk. His baptism at Stepney and the 1871 and 1881 censuses all say London, and in a lodging house the householder usually answered for visitors, so London is the better reading.

sections.heading: Robert William FitzMaurice
sections.text: On 14 September 1861, a surveyor, he married Fanny Mary Falcke at St Mary's, Battersea. The register calls his father John a gentleman, and her father William Gottlob Falcke a manufacturer. In 1871 he was a surveyor and contractor at Little Bromwich, Aston, born in Stepney. In 1881 he was a granite merchant and contractor at Sutton Road, Aston Manor. He died at 16 York Road, Edgbaston, on 10 May 1895, aged 64. The estate was 12,921 pounds 4 shillings and 9 pence. The executors were his widow Fanny Mary and their sons John Rupert, a quarry owner, and Walter, a contractor.

sections.heading: Fanny Mary FitzMaurice, nee Falcke
sections.text: Born 3 December 1836, Battersea. Baptised 29 January 1837, as Mary Fanny. Died 25 October 1917, Erdington. She was the youngest child of William Gottlob Falcke, a potter, and Elizabeth. A line in the 1871 census that gives her birthplace as France is a mistake. The baptism, the 1851 census and the 1881 census all give Battersea. She was 80 when she died at Erdington. In 1901 she was a widow living on her own means in Chester Road, Boldmere, Sutton Coldfield. With her were her son Arthur, 33, a manager for a road contractor (as far as the entry can be read), a granddaughter, Mary K. Hendrick, 13, and two servants. She gave her age as 60, about four years too young. Her address when she died in 1917 was The Nest, Chester Road, Erdington. In 1861 the Falcke and Turner household lived at 2 Elm Terrace, Wandsworth Road.

sections.heading: William Gottlob Falcke
sections.text: Born abroad about 1793. Potter at Battersea. Buried 27 August 1849, St Mary's, Battersea, aged 56. William Gottlob Falcke married Eliza Macfarlin at St Mary's, Battersea, on 15 October 1817. Their children were baptised at St Luke's, Chelsea and St Mary's, Battersea between 1818 and 1837: Eliza Caroline (1818), Henrietta (1820), Jane (1822), William Gottlob (1824), Emma (1826), Charlotte (1828), Elizabeth (1830), Frederick Henry (1832), Emily Catherine (1834) and Mary Fanny, later known as Fanny Mary (1837). William was a potter. The 1841 census says he was born in foreign parts. He was buried at Battersea on 27 August 1849, aged 56. By Fanny's wedding in 1861 he was described as a manufacturer.

sections.heading: Elizabeth Falcke
sections.text: Probably born at Harrow about 1796 or 1797. Recorded as Eliza Macfarlin in 1817. In 1851 his widow Elizabeth, 54, born at Harrow, was working as a potter at Bolingbroke Gardens, Battersea, employing 3 men and 2 boys. Her death has not been tied to a certificate.

sections.heading: The children at Battersea in 1841
sections.text: The 1841 household lists Eliza (20), Jane (15), Charlotte (13), Elizabeth (11), Frederick (9), Emily (7) and Fanny (4). Those ages are as the census wrote them. Five of the daughters married at St Mary's, Battersea: Henrietta to Whitford Henry Nichols, an accountant, in 1840; Eliza Caroline to Samuel Knight, a clerk of Wandsworth, in 1845; Charlotte to James Cooper, a master mariner, on 19 October 1850, with her brother Frederick and sister Jane as witnesses; Jane to John Peacock Turner in 1858; and Fanny Mary to Robert William FitzMaurice in 1861.

sections.heading: Edward's brothers and sister
sections.text: Six births name the mother as Falcke, in the King's Norton and Aston districts. They are probably Robert and Fanny's children. William Robert, summer 1862, King's Norton, volume 6c, page 406. He is not in the 1871 household. Eliza Ada, early 1864, King's Norton, volume 6c, page 466. With the family in 1871 and 1881. John Rupert, spring 1865, King's Norton, volume 6c, page 447. Called Rupert J. in 1871. A quarry owner, and an executor, in 1895. Died at Leicester on 21 September 1949, aged 84. The estate was 56,789 pounds 19 shillings and 2 pence. Arthur Percy, summer 1867, Aston, volume 6d, page 352. Walter, late 1869, Aston, volume 6d, page 345. A contractor, and an executor, in 1895. A Walter registered at Aston in 1872, mother Stevens, is a different family. Edward Dixon, born 21 October 1872, Aston, volume 6d, page 396, and baptised at Ward End on 19 June 1873.

sections.heading: Edward's brothers and sister
sections.text: Harry, aged 5, is in the 1871 household at Little Bromwich. His place in the family is not settled. References for every entry are on the sources page. Historic addresses of people who have died are shown in full.

sections.heading: Reg's mother, brother and sisters
sections.text: The medallion inscribed Edith Madeleine Fitzmaurice is Reg's mother, Edith Madeline Spencer, not his sister. She and Edward Dixon had four children. Three of them grew up.

sections.heading: Edith Madeline FitzMaurice, nee Spencer
sections.text: Probably born about 1866 to 1869, Islington. Married 2 August 1897. Probably died early 1929, Bridge district, Kent, aged 61.

sections.heading: Edith Madeline FitzMaurice, nee Spencer
sections.text: In 1891 she was Edith Spencer, 22, a governess, born in Islington, living with her widowed mother Caroline, a lodging house keeper, at 15 Mornington Place, St Pancras. The house number may read 15b. Her father was Charles Spencer, a builder and contractor, already dead by then. Caroline witnessed the wedding at St Matthew's, Brixton, where Edith's age was written as 24. In 1911 the census says she was 38 and born at St Anne, Soho, and that four children had been born, of whom three were living. At the end of 1923 she came to London with Reg and Eileen. The passenger list of the P and O liner Bendigo, which called at Durban and Cape Town on its way from Australia, has Edith Fitzmaurice, 51, Baron, a student, 19, and Eileen, 16, landing in London on 28 December 1923, giving their address as 140A Clapham Road, London S.W. (the number is hard to read) and their home as South Africa. Edward Dixon had sailed back to the Cape from Southampton a week earlier. A Cape Times list of August 1923 has a Miss E. S. Fitzmaurice and an E. M. Fitzmaurice leaving Cape Town on the Bendigo, probably Eileen and her mother, but the dates do not match the December landing and the question is still open. She came back to England on the Saxon, landing at Southampton on 24 November 1925, aged 53 by her own account, and gave 55 Seymour Street, Higher Tranmere, Birkenhead as her address. The death index in 1929 says 61. The 1891 age and the death age agree with about 1866 to 1869. The later ages look younger. Her birth registration has not been found. A birth of Edith Maria Spencer at Islington in 1866 is a different family.

sections.heading: Edith Madeline FitzMaurice, nee Spencer
sections.text: Caroline was probably with Edward and Edith in Brixton in 1901. She was born in Islington, about 1843 to 1849. An 1881 entry sometimes suggested for her is not used here. In April 1911 a Caroline Spencer, 67, a widow born in Islington, was keeping a lodging house at 6 Cathles Road, Balham Hill, with her niece May Cobon, 25, a shorthand typist. She was probably Edith's mother: her age, birthplace, widowhood and work all fit, though the page does not name Edith. Her death has not been found.

sections.heading: Edith Marjorie FitzMaurice
sections.text: Probably late 1899, Greenwich district, to summer 1900, Lewisham district. Mother's maiden name Spencer. Volume 1d, page 1075 for the birth, and volume 1d, page 707 for the death, aged under a year. She is the child who had died by 1911. She was named after her mother, and she is not the woman in the medallion.

sections.heading: Edward Robert FitzMaurice, called Bob (1901 to 1981)
sections.text: Probably spring 1901, Lambeth district. Died 7 May 1981, Port Elizabeth, South Africa.

sections.heading: Edward Robert FitzMaurice, called Bob (1901 to 1981)
sections.text: The beach photograph is labelled Reg, Bob and their father Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice. It was probably taken about 1908 to 1910 on the Kent coast. Edward Robert, mother's maiden name Spencer, was registered in the Lambeth district in the June quarter of 1901, volume 1d, page 503. He is probably Bob. He was probably the boy of 15 who sailed to Cape Town with his mother in August 1916. No later record of him has been found in England. The family always believed that Bob stayed in South Africa, and the records now show that he did. On 30 October 1925, aged 24, he married Eileen Alice Yallop, 23, born in South Africa, at St George's Cathedral, Cape Town, by licence. He was a tramway engineer living at "Auleta", Three Anchor Bay, and she lived at 7 Bertram Road, Sea Point. One of the witnesses was J. A. Cartwright.

sections.heading: Edward Robert FitzMaurice, called Bob (1901 to 1981)
sections.text: Their first son, Edward Scott FitzMaurice, was born on 29 April 1926 and baptised on 25 July 1926 in the parish of Woodstock, Cape Town. The family was then living at 17 Berkley Street, Gardens, Cape Town (the house number may be 14), and Bob was still a tramway engineer. The godparents were Joseph Allan Cartwright, Thomas Baker and Bertha Scott. Edward Scott died on 9 August 1935, aged 9; his death is known from an index and from the title of his estate file in the Cape Town archives. Bob and Eileen had two more sons, both baptised in Cape Town: Lawrence John FitzMaurice in 1932 and Derek Anthony FitzMaurice in 1934.

sections.heading: Edward Robert FitzMaurice, called Bob (1901 to 1981)
sections.text: Bob died at Port Elizabeth on 7 May 1981, aged about 80, and his death was registered in Cape Town on 27 May. The index to his death notice names his father, Edward Dickson (Dixon) FitzMaurice, his mother Edith, his wife Eileen Alice, and his sons Laurence John and Derek Anthony (indexed as "Serel Anthony"). The death notice image itself is not open to view. Two undated Cape Supreme Court civil cases that he brought against a Raymond William Wilson are probably his too.

sections.heading: Baron Reginald FitzMaurice, called Reg
sections.text: Probably 26 May 1904, Wandsworth district. Died 31 March 1977, Hayes.

sections.heading: Baron Reginald FitzMaurice, called Reg
sections.text: Baron is a forename, not a title. The birth was registered in the September quarter of 1904, Wandsworth, volume 1d, page 670, mother Spenser. In 1911 he was 6 and at school at Whitstable. He was probably the boy of 12 who sailed to Cape Town with his mother in August 1916. He came back to London with his mother and Eileen on the Bendigo, landing on 28 December 1923, when he was listed as Baron Fitzmaurice, a student, aged 19. Early in 1925 Reg made a short trip to Canada. On 7 February 1925 a Baron Fitzmaurice, a clerk, of 7 North Lane, Clapham Common, sailed from Liverpool on the Canadian Pacific liner Montrose. On 15 February the Canadian immigration officers at Saint John, New Brunswick, recorded him as Baron Reg Fitzmaurice, 20, single, born in London, a clerk who meant to take up farming, going to the Y.M.C.A. in Saint John. His nearest relative at home was an E. Fitzmaurice of 7 North Side, Clapham. Three weeks later he was on his way back: he left Saint John on the Marburn on 6 March and landed at Southampton on 14 March 1925, now listed as "Banon Reg." Fitzmaurice, 20, a salesman, going to 7 North Street, Clapham Common. The forename Baron, his age, his birth in London and the Clapham Common address on all three lists make it very likely that this was Reg. The British list gives his age as 30, which is probably a slip for 20. Why he went, and why he came home so soon, is not known. No record places him in Canada before February 1925: he is not in the 1921 census of Canada, and no earlier sailing or arrival has been found. Nobody in the family seems to have heard of the trip. From then on the electoral registers follow him: 26 Turret Grove, Clapham, in 1925 and 1926; 34 Blythe Road, Hammersmith, from 1931 to 1933; 113 Bourne Avenue, Harlington, in 1936 and 1937; and from 1938 42 Nestles Avenue, Hayes, where he lived until he died in 1977. Reg probably married again after Lilian's death in 1947: from 1949 the electoral registers also name an Elizabeth C. Fitzmaurice, probably his second wife. Nothing more is known about her yet. He probably married Lilian Maud Mary Bennett in the December quarter of 1927, Hammersmith, volume 1a, page 661. He gave Patricia away on 11 February 1950. The death was registered at Hillingdon. The probate calendar places him at Hayes, with an estate of 24,427 pounds. A bow-tie studio portrait has no name on it, and it is not identified as him.

sections.heading: Eileen Sybil FitzMaurice, called Auntie Babs (confirmed by the family)
sections.text: Born late 1907, Blean district, Kent. Died early 1996, Canterbury, probably aged 88.

sections.heading: Eileen Sybil FitzMaurice, called Auntie Babs (confirmed by the family)
sections.text: The youngest of Edward Dixon and Edith's children, Eileen was 3 at Whitstable in 1911. She probably sailed to Cape Town with her mother and brothers in August 1916, aged 8, and the family photo labelled Auntie Babs, South Africa shows her as a girl there. She came back to London from South Africa with her mother and Reg on the Bendigo, landing on 28 December 1923, aged 16. She married Leslie Hugh Simmons, secretary of the Corinth Hockey Club, at Staines in the summer of 1936. The newspaper named her as the daughter of the late Edward Dixon Fitzmaurice, formerly of Cape Town. For several years Eileen lived with her brother Reg and his wife Lilian: the electoral registers list the three of them at 34 Blythe Road, Hammersmith, in 1931 and 1933, and at 113 Bourne Avenue, Harlington, in 1936, the year she married. Banns for her marriage to Leslie Simmons were read at Harlington in July 1936, but the entry is marked cancelled; the wedding itself was reported in the Buckinghamshire Advertiser that September. By 1939 she and Leslie lived at 55 Bourne Avenue, Hayes, on the same road where she had lived with Reg. As Auntie Babs she was at Pat's wedding in 1950 with Uncle Leslie. In 1984 she married Ralph Hallawell in Kent, and she probably died at Canterbury in early 1996.

sections.heading: Eileen Sybil FitzMaurice, called Auntie Babs (confirmed by the family)
sections.text: The parents of Edward Dixon are on the Falcke page. The citations are on the sources page.

sections.heading: Lilian Bennett's family
sections.text: Lilian Maud Mary Bennett, Pat's mother, was born about March 1900 at Bodmin. She was the youngest surviving child of Charles Bennett and Annie, probably Matilda Ann Nicholls Grigg.

sections.heading: Lilian Maud Mary FitzMaurice, nee Bennett
sections.text: About March 1900, Bodmin. Probably died late 1947, Uxbridge district, aged 47. The birth index, June quarter 1900, Bodmin, volume 5c, page 64, names her mother as Grigg. In June 1921 she was 21 years and 3 months, born at Bodmin, a clerk at the Claims Record Office, boarding at Hampton Hill. She probably married Baron Reginald FitzMaurice in the December quarter of 1927, Hammersmith, volume 1a, page 661. She probably died in the December quarter of 1947, Uxbridge, volume 5f, page 103, aged 47. The Uxbridge district covered Hayes, which is why the 1950 album calls her the late Mrs R. Fitzmaurice. No will and no grave have been found. A memory that she died while Pat was a young child does not fit an age of about 18.

sections.heading: Charles and Annie
sections.text: Charles Bennett was born at Egloshayle, Cornwall, about 1849 to 1851. The 1911 census says Slades, Egloshayle. He was a tailor in 1891, a general labourer at 1 Honey Street, Bodmin, in 1901, and a tailor and outfitter in 1911. Annie was probably Matilda Ann Nicholls Grigg, born in the St Columb district in the March quarter of 1864, volume 5c, page 131, mother's maiden name Stephens. They probably married in the September quarter of 1882, in the Stoke Damerel district, volume 5b, page 573, where Charles Bennett and Annie Grigg share a page.

sections.heading: Charles and Annie
sections.text: In 1911 they were living apart in Bodmin. Annie, who kept a draper's shop, described herself as a widow, though Charles was alive in the same town with their son Frank. Both forms say 11 children had been born, 8 were living and 3 had died. Annie died in the June quarter of 1912 at Bodmin, aged 48, registered as Matilda Ann Nicholls Bennett, volume 5c, page 89. Charles probably died at Bodmin on 5 December 1925, aged 77. Administration of an estate of 296 pounds 1 shilling and 4 pence was granted to May Bennett, a spinster. That grant does not show which daughter she was.

sections.heading: The eleven children
sections.text: All eleven births were registered at Bodmin with mother's maiden name Grigg. Three died as infants, which matches the 1911 count. James Alfred, late 1883, volume 5c, page 79. Probably died early 1884, aged 0. Gilbert Nicholls, late 1884, volume 5c, page 77. A tailor's apprentice in 1901, and a bootfitter in 1911. Charles Reginald, late 1886, volume 5c, page 71. A draper's apprentice in 1901. The census calls him Reginald. Minnie Elizabeth, spring 1888, volume 5c, page 72. A milliner, single, with her mother in 1911. She is not Amanda's Auntie May. Harry, spring 1890, volume 5c, page 77. Arthur Sidney, spring 1892, volume 5c, page 65. Called Sidney in 1901. He is not Sidney George Andrews. Frederick Cyril, spring 1894, volume 5c, page 77. Probably died in 1895, aged 1. William Frances, late 1895, volume 5c, page 69. Known as Francis, and as Frank. With his father in 1911.

sections.heading: The eleven children
sections.text: Cecil Floyd Chester, summer 1898, volume 5c, page 70. Called Floyd. He probably married Ethel G. Clark in 1924, in the Farnham district, and he probably died in 1970, in the Plymouth district. Lilian Maud Mary, about March 1900, volume 5c, page 64. Harold Victor, spring 1902, volume 5c, page 61. Probably died in 1904, aged 1. The 1901 census gives 1 Honey Street. Citations are on the sources page.

sections.heading: Andrews, Stacey and Walter
sections.text: Henry George Andrews, Ron's father, was the only child of a Totternhoe baker and a Stacey from Leavesden. The line runs back through Aldenham, Bushey, Denham and Letchmore Heath.

sections.heading: Henry George, Herbert and Sidney
sections.text: Henry George Andrews was born at St Albans in April 1889 and baptised at St Albans Abbey on 9 June 1889. The birth index, June quarter 1889, St Albans, volume 3a, page 559, names his mother as Stacey. The 1939 Register probably gives the day as 8 April. On 18 April 1915, aged 25, he married Rosina Maud Cousins at St Andrew's, Plaistow. In 1911 he was a sawyer's labourer at Canning Town. In 1921 he was a dock labourer for the Port of London Authority at the Royal Albert Docks. In 1939 he was an explosive worker at the Royal filling factory, Woolwich. On 7 December 1915, less than eight months after his wedding, Henry George Andrews attested at Stratford for the Army Service Corps, signing on for the duration of the war. He gave his address as 23 Sutton Court Road, Plaistow, his age as 26 and his trade as clerk, and said he was married. His number was 220072, later written T4/220072. His medal card shows that he received the British War Medal and the Victory Medal. His full service file has 18 pages, several of them burnt at the edges. He was placed in the Army Reserve the day after he attested and was called up on 6 November 1916. The next day he joined "K" Company of the Army Service Corps as a private. On 13 November he was issued his uniform and kit at the Corps mobilisation store at Aldershot, and he was later transferred to the Motor Transport depot. He was stamped as embarked for France on 1 January 1917 and served there with the Expeditionary Force from 9 January 1917 to 6 November 1919, nearly three years. His papers record a tattoo on his left forearm and give his religion as Church of England, and his wife Rosina, at 23 Sutton Court Road, as his next of kin. His discharge papers give his trade as packer and loader. He passed through the dispersal unit at Crystal Palace on 5 November 1919 and was transferred to the Class Z Army Reserve on 3 December 1919. In August 1920 the Ministry of Pensions asked for his papers. The file does not say why, and the surviving pages record no wound and no pension. He, Rosina and their son Sidney George were killed at 23 Sutton Court Road, Plaistow, on 19 April 1941.

sections.heading: Henry George, Herbert and Sidney
sections.text: The war-dead records name the house: 23 Sutton Court Road, Plaistow, in the West Ham county borough, on 19 April 1941. Henry was 52, Rosina 59 and Sidney 18. The wedding album says East Ham, which is the next borough. The war-dead records say Plaistow. Sidney was born in the West Ham district in the spring of 1923, volume 4a, page 150, mother Cousins, and in 1939 he was a junior clerk at a hardwood merchant. Herbert William, the elder brother, was born in the West Ham district in 1916, volume 4a, page 180. He was 4 in 1921 and, in 1939, an explosive worker at Woolwich with his father. He probably married Christina M. Knight in 1940, in the East Ham district. Their daughter is Christine Ellis, Amanda's first cousin. His death has not been found, so the exact day of birth on the 1939 Register is not published. Ronald's own birth is not published here.

sections.heading: Herbert Andrews
sections.text: 12 November 1865 on the 1939 Register. Totternhoe. Probably died early 1951.

sections.heading: Herbert Andrews
sections.text: He was 5 at Totternhoe in 1871, son of George and Alice. At 15 he was probably a page in a household at Wimbledon. On 17 May 1888, aged 22, he married Lucy Stacey at Bushey. His father is named as George Andrews. He was a journeyman baker: at Hemel Hempstead in 1901, at Canning Town in 1911, and on night work for a bakery in Plymouth Road, Canning Town, in 1921, when he and Lucy were at Plaistow. In 1911 Henry, 21, worked as a sawyer's labourer at a saw mill and lived with his parents at 40 Fisher Street, Canning Town. His father Herbert, 45, was a journeyman baker; his mother Lucy was 46. The form says they had been married 23 years and had one child, so Henry George was their only child. In 1939 he was a widower and a retired baker at West Ham. He probably died in the March quarter of 1951 in the Essex South Western district, volume 5a, page 209, aged 84. That age is about a year younger than the 1939 birth date.

sections.heading: Lucy Andrews, nee Stacey
sections.text: Spring 1865, Watford district. Probably died 1932, West Ham, aged 67. Born in the June quarter of 1865, Watford Union, volume 3a, page 333, mother's maiden name Walter. The censuses give Watford and, in 1921, Leavesden. She was 6 at Aldenham in 1871. In 1881 Lucy Stacey, 16, born at Aldenham, was a general servant in the household of Francis Miller in Denmark Street, Watford. She probably died in the September quarter of 1932, West Ham, volume 4a, page 153, aged 67.

sections.heading: George and Alice, of Totternhoe
sections.text: George Andrews was an agricultural labourer, born at Totternhoe about 1843. In 1871 he was 28, with Alice, 33, also born at Totternhoe, and sons Herbert and Albert. Elizabeth Field, aged 65 and born at Stanbridge, was in the household and described as mother. By 1881 the family was at Aldenham. George was 38. With them were Alice, Albert, Isabell, Rose and Mary, and Elizabeth Field, now described as his mother-in-law. Alice's maiden name was probably Field, and Elizabeth was probably her mother, born about 1805 or 1806. George and Alice married in the last three months of 1863 in the Luton district; the marriage index lists only the two of them on that register page. In 1881 and again in 1891 the family lived at High Cross, Aldenham. In 1891 George, 48, was a general labourer and Alice was 53. Their son Albert, 22, was a greengrocer, Rose, 16, was a general servant, and Lilie, 8, was at school. The census index places them at Kemprow, but Kemprow is the next house on the page. Elizabeth Field was no longer with them. She may be the Elizabeth Field, born about 1804, whose death was registered at Watford late in 1888, but that has not been checked. Next door lived a baker's servant of 16, Daniel Field, born at Bricket Wood. He may have been one of Alice's relatives; nothing yet shows it.

sections.heading: The Staceys and the Walters
sections.text: Henry Stacey, Lucy's father, was baptised at Denham, Buckinghamshire, on 16 March 1834, son of Henry and Ann. He was 7 at Denham in 1841. On 5 June 1858 he married Mary Walter at Leavesden. He gave his age as 24, a little older than the baptism. He was a farm labourer. In 1861 he and Mary, with their first child Emily, were visiting at Abbots Langley. In 1871 they were at Aldenham, and in 1881 and 1891 at Bushey. By 1901 Henry and Mary were at Ham Farm, Aldenham. Henry, 67, was a general carman or carrier (the word is hard to read) and an employer. Their sons Henry, a garden labourer, and Arthur and Herbert, both horse drivers, lived with them. So did their daughter Louisa with her husband Arthur Robinson, an estate painter, and George Hitch, a boarder from Denham.

sections.heading: The Staceys and the Walters
sections.text: His parents, Henry and Ann, were agricultural labourers at Denham. The 1841 household includes Emma, Stephen, Henry, Mary, Sally, Maria and George. They were probably born about 1801 to 1806. The 1851 census gives the elder Henry's birthplace as Chalfont.

sections.heading: The Staceys and the Walters
sections.text: Mary Stacey, nee Walter, was baptised at Aldenham on 4 November 1838, daughter of Robert and Mary Walter. In 1841 she was 2, at Letchmore Heath, with her parents and four older brothers and sisters: Rachel, Rebecca, James and Robert. Robert was an agricultural labourer, aged 32. The marriage age of 21 is a little high. Lucy's birth index names the mother as Walter, so this Mary was her mother. In 1861 Robert Walter, 52, was a carrier at Letchmore Heath, with his wife Mary and their younger children Ann, William and Lucy. Mary had married three years before. The census index spells the name Waller, but the page says Walter, and the names and ages match the family at High Cross in 1851. The Cousins side of Ron's family, including Auntie May, is on the Cousins page.

sections.heading: Cousins, Gall, and Auntie May
sections.text: Rosina Maud Andrews was born Rosina Maud Cousins, at Bermondsey, on 14 November 1881. Her mother was Annie Cousins, nee Gall. Her younger sister May Florence Cousins was Auntie May.

sections.heading: William Cousins and Anne Gall
sections.text: Married 15 January 1871, St Philip's, Stepney. William was probably baptised on 1 December 1850 at St John, Hackney, the son of William Cousins and his wife Elizabeth. At the baptism his father was a porter. In 1861 the family was probably living at Mile End Old Town, and William's brothers and sisters included Amelia. His father was a messenger in that census (St John, Hackney, baptisms, Ancestry record 2494246; 1861 census, RG9/293, folio 180, page 18, Mile End Old Town, Ancestry record 5902323).

sections.heading: William Cousins and Anne Gall
sections.text: On 15 January 1871 William was 21 and a clerk. Anne was 24. The register names his father as William Cousins, a clerk, and does not say the father was dead. Her father, John Gall, was a brewer, and he had died before the wedding. By 1881 William was a wharf foreman in Bermondsey. Annie was born about 1846 at Thetford, Norfolk. The birth index gives the mother's maiden name as Gall, or Galle, for all eight children, so the maiden name is certain.

sections.heading: William Cousins and Anne Gall
sections.text: Annie probably died in the September quarter of 1900 in the West Ham district, volume 4a, page 76, aged 53. She is gone by the 1901 census. William was later a dock labourer. In 1921 he was a retired dock labourer, living with Rosina and Henry George at Plaistow. He probably died in the December quarter of 1922 in the West Ham district, volume 4a, page 53, aged 71. Where John Gall himself came from has not been settled, and the guesses are not used here. By 1911 William Cousins, a widower of 61 and an assistant dock foreman, lived at 23 Sutton Court Road, Plaistow, with his unmarried daughter Amelia Ann, 34. This is the house where Rosina and Henry George later lived with him, and where they were killed in 1941.
